vert_L5.note: The largest vertebra, with a wedge-shaped body that sits on the sloping sacrum; its large transverse processes are tied to the pelvis by the iliolumbar ligaments.
vert_L5.lesion: Spondylolysis (a defect of the pars interarticularis) is commonest here and can allow L5 to slip forward on S1 (spondylolisthesis), narrowing the L5 foramina.

cervical_plexus.note: Loops between the ventral rami of C1-C4 beside the upper cervical vertebrae. Its sensory branches (lesser occipital C2, great auricular C2-C3, transverse cervical C2-C3, supraclavicular C3-C4) fan out from the middle of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid (Erb's point) to the scalp behind the ear, the ear and angle of the jaw, the front of the neck and the skin over the clavicle and shoulder. The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) supplies the infrahyoid muscles; the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is its main motor branch.
cervical_plexus.lesion: Its sensory branches are blocked at Erb's point for neck surgery. Injury in neck operations numbs the ear lobe (great auricular nerve) or the skin of the neck.

phrenic_nerve.note: C3, C4 and C5 (mainly C4) join on the front of scalenus anterior; the nerve runs down in front of the subclavian artery into the thorax, then over the pericardium to the diaphragm, which is its only motor target. It also carries sensation from the central diaphragm, mediastinal pleura and pericardium. The left nerve is longer and curves round the heart.
phrenic_nerve.lesion: Damage paralyses one half of the diaphragm (raised hemidiaphragm on X-ray, breathlessness lying flat if both sides). Irritation of the diaphragm is felt at the shoulder tip (C4 dermatome). A cord injury above C3-C5 removes breathing.

brachial_plexus.note: Ventral rami of C5-T1 (roots) form three trunks between scalenus anterior and medius (upper C5-C6, middle C7, lower C8-T1, the lower lying on the first rib); each trunk splits behind the clavicle into an anterior and a posterior division; in the axilla the divisions form three cords named by their position around the axillary artery: lateral (anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks), medial (anterior division of the lower trunk) and posterior (all posterior divisions). This regular arrangement was found in 84% of 3,055 limbs; 11% were prefixed (contribution from C4) and 1% postfixed (from T2); the division-to-cord pattern was regular in 96% (Benes 2021).
brachial_plexus.lesion: Upper trunk injury (Erb palsy, C5-C6; birth traction or a fall onto the shoulder): arm hangs adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended, weak shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. Lower trunk injury (Klumpke palsy, C8-T1; traction on an abducted arm, apical lung tumour): weak hand muscles with clawing, ulnar-side numbness, and Horner syndrome if the T1 sympathetic fibres are damaged. The thoracic outlet over the first rib can compress the lower trunk.

musculocutaneous_nerve.note: From the lateral cord; pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps and brachialis, which it supplies, and ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
musculocutaneous_nerve.lesion: Isolated injury is uncommon: weak elbow flexion and supination (biceps), reduced biceps reflex, numbness of the lateral forearm.

median_nerve.note: Formed by a root from the lateral cord and a root from the medial cord in front of the axillary artery; runs down the medial arm beside the brachial artery to the cubital fossa (drawn to the elbow). In the forearm and hand it supplies most forearm flexors, the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals, and the skin of the palmar thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger.
median_nerve.lesion: Compression in the carpal tunnel (the commonest entrapment neuropathy) causes night-time tingling of the thumb to ring finger and, later, thenar wasting. A lesion at the elbow also weakens flexion of the thumb, index and middle fingers (the hand of benediction when trying to make a fist).

ulnar_nerve.note: From the medial cord; runs down the medial arm, passes behind the medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel) and supplies flexor carpi ulnaris, part of flexor digitorum profundus and most small hand muscles, and the skin of the little finger and half the ring finger.
ulnar_nerve.lesion: Compression at the elbow or wrist: numbness of the little finger and half the ring finger, weak finger spreading and pinch (Froment sign), wasting of the first dorsal interosseous and clawing of the ring and little fingers.

radial_nerve.note: The largest branch of the posterior cord; winds round the back of the humerus in the spiral groove to the front of the lateral epicondyle. It supplies triceps, the wrist and finger extensors and brachioradialis, and the skin of the back of the arm, forearm and hand.
radial_nerve.lesion: Compression or a humeral shaft fracture in the spiral groove causes wrist drop and finger drop with sparing of triceps, and numbness over the back of the first web space ('Saturday night palsy').

axillary_nerve.note: From the posterior cord; passes backwards through the quadrangular space round the surgical neck of the humerus to supply deltoid and teres minor and the skin over the lower deltoid.
axillary_nerve.lesion: Injured by shoulder dislocation or fracture of the surgical neck: weak abduction beyond the first degrees and a numb patch over the lower deltoid (the 'regimental badge' area).

long_thoracic_nerve.note: From the roots, behind the plexus, down the side of the chest wall on serratus anterior, which it supplies (holds the scapula against the chest).
long_thoracic_nerve.lesion: Damage (axillary surgery, carrying heavy loads on the shoulder, neuralgic amyotrophy) causes winging of the scapula, seen when pushing against a wall.

suprascapular_nerve.note: From the upper trunk; runs back to the suprascapular notch to supply supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
suprascapular_nerve.lesion: Entrapment at the notch on the upper border of the scapula or at the spinoglenoid notch weakens the start of shoulder abduction and external rotation, with wasting above and below the spine of the scapula.

intercostal_nerves.note: The ventral rami of the thoracic nerves run forward below each rib in the costal groove, with the intercostal vein and artery above them, supplying the intercostal muscles, the skin of the chest wall and, from T7 to T12, the muscles and skin of the abdominal wall. Most of T1 joins the brachial plexus.
intercostal_nerves.lesion: Shingles (herpes zoster) and diabetic radiculopathy cause band-like pain in one dermatome. Because the nerve and vessels run under the rib, needles for chest drains and nerve blocks are passed just above a rib.

iliohypogastric_nerve.note: Leaves the lateral border of psoas, crosses in front of quadratus lumborum and runs round the flank above the iliac crest into the lower abdominal wall; supplies the lower oblique and transverse muscles and the skin above the pubis and of the upper buttock.
iliohypogastric_nerve.lesion: Injury in lower abdominal or hernia incisions causes numbness or burning pain above the pubis. Fusion with the ilioinguinal nerve was the commonest variant (9.6% of 260 sides; Benes 2024).

ilioinguinal_nerve.note: Runs parallel to and below the iliohypogastric nerve and through the inguinal canal to the skin of the upper medial thigh and the root of the penis and scrotum or the mons and labia.
ilioinguinal_nerve.lesion: Injured or trapped in hernia repair and low transverse incisions: groin pain and numbness of the upper inner thigh and genital skin.

genitofemoral_nerve.note: Pierces the front of psoas and runs down on it. Its genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring (cremaster muscle, scrotal or labial skin); its femoral branch supplies the skin below the middle of the inguinal ligament. In about half of 260 sides it already left psoas divided into its two branches (48.1%; Benes 2024).
genitofemoral_nerve.lesion: One of its two branches is the motor limb of the cremasteric reflex. Injury in hernia surgery causes groin and genital pain.

lateral_femoral_cutaneous_nerve.note: Leaves the lateral border of psoas, crosses iliacus and enters the thigh under or through the inguinal ligament close to the anterior superior iliac spine; purely sensory to the anterolateral thigh. It was the least variable lumbar plexus nerve outside psoas (typical in 95.0%; Benes 2024).
lateral_femoral_cutaneous_nerve.lesion: Compression near the anterior superior iliac spine (tight belts, obesity, pregnancy) causes meralgia paraesthetica: burning numbness of the outer thigh with no weakness.

femoral_nerve.note: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus; forms in psoas, leaves its lateral border, runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus and enters the thigh under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery; supplies iliacus, quadriceps, sartorius and pectineus, the skin of the front of the thigh and, through the saphenous nerve, the medial leg and foot.
femoral_nerve.lesion: Damage (pelvic surgery, retroperitoneal or psoas haematoma in people on anticoagulants) causes weak knee extension with the knee giving way, a lost knee reflex and numbness of the front of the thigh and the medial leg.

obturator_nerve.note: Leaves the medial border of psoas at the pelvic brim, runs along the side wall of the pelvis and through the obturator canal to the adductor muscles and a patch of skin on the medial thigh. It often branched before the canal (40.4%), and an accessory obturator nerve was present in 9.2% (Benes 2024).
obturator_nerve.lesion: Injury in pelvic surgery or childbirth weakens hip adduction (unstable gait) and numbs the medial thigh; a hernia through the canal it passes can cause pain down the inner thigh (Howship-Romberg sign).

lumbosacral_trunk.note: Part of the L4 ventral ramus joins all of L5 and descends over the sacral ala into the pelvis to join S1: the link between the lumbar and sacral plexuses.
lumbosacral_trunk.lesion: It can be compressed by the fetal head during labour against the pelvic brim, causing foot drop after delivery (maternal obstetric palsy).

sacral_plexus.note: The lumbosacral trunk and the ventral rami of S1-S4, which leave the anterior sacral foramina, unite on the front of piriformis. Its main branches leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen: the sciatic nerve, the superior and inferior gluteal nerves, the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve and the pudendal nerve. S2-S4 also carry the pelvic parasympathetic outflow to bladder, bowel and genitals.
sacral_plexus.lesion: Pelvic tumours, sacral fractures and pelvic radiotherapy can damage it, causing buttock and leg weakness, leg numbness and sphincter problems.

sciatic_nerve.note: The largest nerve of the body: leaves the pelvis below piriformis and runs down the back of the thigh between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity, supplying the hamstrings; above the knee it divides into the tibial and common fibular (peroneal) nerves, which supply all muscles below the knee and most of the skin of the leg and foot. Drawn to the mid thigh.
sciatic_nerve.lesion: Injury from hip surgery or dislocation, a misplaced buttock injection or a pelvic fracture causes weakness of knee flexion and of all movement below the knee, often worst for ankle dorsiflexion (foot drop, because the fibular part is more vulnerable), with numbness below the knee except the medial side.

superior_gluteal_nerve.note: Leaves the pelvis above piriformis and supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae (the hip abductors that hold the pelvis level when walking).
superior_gluteal_nerve.lesion: Damage (hip surgery, injections) causes a Trendelenburg gait: the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg.

inferior_gluteal_nerve.note: Leaves the pelvis below piriformis and supplies gluteus maximus, the main hip extensor.
inferior_gluteal_nerve.lesion: Weakness makes rising from a chair and climbing stairs difficult.

pudendal_nerve.note: Leaves the pelvis below piriformis, hooks round the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen and runs forward in the pudendal (Alcock) canal to the perineum: external anal and urethral sphincters, pelvic floor, skin of the perineum and genitals.
pudendal_nerve.lesion: Stretch in childbirth or compression (long-distance cycling, entrapment in its canal on the side wall of the ischioanal fossa) causes perineal pain made worse by sitting, numbness and sometimes incontinence.

posterior_femoral_cutaneous_nerve.note: Leaves below piriformis beside the sciatic nerve and supplies the skin of the back of the thigh, the lower buttock and part of the perineum.
posterior_femoral_cutaneous_nerve.lesion: Injury causes numbness of the back of the thigh, often together with sciatic or pudendal symptoms.

psoas_major.note: Arises from the bodies and transverse processes of T12-L4 and the discs between them, runs down beside the lumbar spine and across the pelvic brim, and inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur; the main hip flexor. The lumbar plexus forms inside it. Its nerve branches arose from L1-L4 (6.3 per muscle on average), with the L2 and L3 branches always present (Mahan 2017). Drawn see-through.
psoas_major.lesion: A psoas abscess or haematoma can compress the femoral nerve; the lateral transpsoas approach to the lumbar spine risks the lumbar plexus nerves inside the muscle.

subclavian_artery.note: The subclavian artery (right from the brachiocephalic trunk, left from the aortic arch) arches over the first rib behind scalenus anterior, gives the vertebral artery from its first part, becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib, surrounded by the cords of the brachial plexus, and the brachial artery below the axilla (drawn to the elbow). Origins are drawn approximately; the heart and aorta are not drawn.
subclavian_artery.lesion: Narrowing of the first part before the vertebral origin can reverse flow in the vertebral artery when the arm works (subclavian steal). The axillary artery can be injured with shoulder dislocation; the thoracic outlet can compress the subclavian artery.

ribs.note: Twelve pairs: the head articulates with the vertebral bodies, the tubercle with the transverse process (ribs 1-10). Ribs 1-7 reach the sternum through their own costal cartilages, 8-10 join the cartilage above (costal margin), 11-12 float. The first rib is short, flat and broad; the subclavian vessels and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus cross it. Drawn with typical proportions.
ribs.lesion: Fractures (most often ribs 4-9) are painful and can puncture the lung; a cervical rib or a tight first rib can compress the lower plexus and subclavian artery (thoracic outlet syndrome).

costal_cartilages.note: Hyaline cartilage bars linking ribs 1-7 to the sternum and ribs 8-10 to the cartilage above; they give the chest wall its spring.
costal_cartilages.lesion: Costochondritis causes chest wall pain that is tender to press; the cartilages calcify with age.

sternum.note: Manubrium, body and xiphoid process. The jugular notch lies at about the level of the T2-T3 vertebrae and the sternal angle (manubriosternal joint), where the second costal cartilage attaches, at about T4-T5; a common landmark for counting ribs.
sternum.lesion: Fractures follow direct blows (steering wheel); median sternotomy is the standard opening for heart surgery.

clavicle.note: An S-shaped strut from the sternum to the acromion that holds the shoulder away from the chest; the subclavian vessels and the divisions of the brachial plexus pass behind and below its middle third.
clavicle.lesion: The commonest fractured bone in children and young adults, usually in the middle third; the vessels and plexus behind it are rarely injured.

sacrum.note: Five fused vertebrae forming the back of the pelvis between the hip bones (sacroiliac joints). Four pairs of anterior and posterior foramina carry the ventral and dorsal rami of S1-S4; the sacral canal ends at the sacral hiatus. Its upper surface slopes forward (sacral slope, 39.5 degrees on average in asymptomatic adults; Sardar 2022).
sacrum.lesion: Sacral insufficiency fractures (older people with osteoporosis) cause low back and buttock pain; sacral tumours (e.g. chordoma) can damage the sacral roots.

coccyx.note: Three to five small fused segments (four drawn) at the end of the column; the filum terminale anchors to it.
coccyx.lesion: Coccydynia: pain on sitting, often after a fall or childbirth.

disc_C2_C3.note: A tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a soft gel core (nucleus pulposus) that cushions load and allows movement between the vertebral bodies. Discs are thickest in the lumbar spine.
disc_C2_C3.lesion: A herniation at this level most often compresses the C3 root. Large central herniations compress the cord (in the neck and chest) or the cauda equina (lumbar).

disc_L1_L2.lesion: A herniation at this level most often compresses the L2 root (posterolateral) or the L1 root (far lateral). Large central herniations compress the cord (in the neck and chest) or the cauda equina (lumbar).

lt_cst.note: Pathway for voluntary movement. It starts in the motor cortex of the precentral gyrus (leg area near the midline, arm area further out) and neighbouring premotor and parietal areas, runs through the corona radiata, the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the middle of the cerebral peduncle, the basilar pons in scattered bundles and the medullary pyramid. In the lower medulla most fibres cross the midline (pyramidal decussation) and descend in the lateral corticospinal tract of the opposite half of the cord; a smaller uncrossed part descends in the anterior corticospinal tract and crosses at the segment where it ends. Fibres end in the grey matter: arm fibres in the cervical enlargement, leg fibres in the lumbosacral enlargement. Blue fibres start on the left, orange fibres on the right, so the colours swap sides where the pathway crosses; white markers show the crossing.
lt_cst.lesion: Above the decussation (cortex, internal capsule, brainstem) a lesion weakens the opposite side of the body; in the cord, below the decussation, it weakens the same side. Upper motor neuron signs: weakness, spasticity, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response (Babinski sign).

lt_dcml.note: Vibration, fine touch and position sense. Large sensory fibres enter through the dorsal root and ascend on the same side in the dorsal columns: fasciculus gracilis (leg and lower trunk, medial) and fasciculus cuneatus (arm and upper trunk, lateral). They end in the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus of the lower medulla. The second neurons send internal arcuate fibres across the midline (sensory decussation) and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, which projects through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus. Here the colours follow the side of the body the fibres carry. Blue fibres start on the left, orange fibres on the right, so the colours swap sides where the pathway crosses; white markers show the crossing.
lt_dcml.lesion: A cord lesion removes vibration and position sense on the same side below it (sensory ataxia, Romberg sign); a lesion above the sensory decussation (medial lemniscus, thalamus, cortex) removes it on the opposite side.

lt_stt.note: Pain, temperature and crude touch. Small sensory fibres end in the dorsal horn; the second neurons cross in the anterior white commissure within about one to two segments and ascend in the anterolateral cord of the opposite side. The tract runs through the lateral medulla and pons, lies beside the medial lemniscus in the midbrain and ends in the ventral posterolateral thalamus, which projects to the postcentral gyrus. It crosses at every level of the cord: the markers show three examples. Colours follow the side of the body. Blue fibres start on the left, orange fibres on the right, so the colours swap sides where the pathway crosses; white markers show the crossing.
lt_stt.lesion: A one-sided cord lesion removes pain and temperature on the opposite side, starting one to two segments below it (Brown-Sequard syndrome). Damage to the crossing fibres in the centre of the cord (syringomyelia) gives a cape-like loss on both sides. A lateral medullary infarct (Wallenberg syndrome) removes pain and temperature from the opposite side of the body.

lt_cpc.note: Carries motor plans from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum. Corticopontine fibres from frontal, parietal and other cortex descend through the internal capsule and cerebral peduncle to the pontine nuclei of the same side. Pontocerebellar fibres cross the midline in the basilar pons (transverse pontine fibres) and enter the opposite cerebellar hemisphere through the middle cerebellar peduncle. Blue fibres start on the left, orange fibres on the right, so the colours swap sides where the pathway crosses; white markers show the crossing.
lt_cpc.lesion: Lesions of the basilar pons or the middle cerebellar peduncle cause ataxia, for example ataxic hemiparesis from a small pontine infarct.

lt_dsct.note: Unconscious position sense from the leg and lower trunk. Sensory fibres end in Clarke's nucleus (dorsal nucleus, about C8 to L3); its axons ascend on the same side at the edge of the dorsolateral cord and enter the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. It does not cross, so each half of the cerebellum receives the same side of the body. Blue fibres carry the left side of the body, orange the right.
lt_dsct.lesion: Together with the double crossing of the cerebellar output, this is why a lesion of one cerebellar hemisphere causes ataxia on the same side of the body.

lt_drt.note: Output of the cerebellar hemisphere. Fibres from the dentate nucleus leave through the superior cerebellar peduncle, cross in the lower midbrain (decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles, at the level of the inferior colliculus), pass through or beside the opposite red nucleus and end in the ventrolateral thalamus, which projects to the motor cortex. That cortex controls the opposite side of the body through the crossed corticospinal tract: two crossings, so each cerebellar hemisphere acts on its own side of the body. Blue fibres start on the left, orange fibres on the right, so the colours swap sides where the pathway crosses; white markers show the crossing.
lt_drt.lesion: A lesion of one cerebellar hemisphere causes ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor on the same side; a lesion of this pathway after its crossing (midbrain, thalamus) affects the opposite side, for example Holmes (rubral) tremor.

skull.note: The bony case of the brain and the frame of the face. The vault and the skull base with the anterior, middle and posterior cranial fossae, the orbits and the upper face are traced here from a CT template registered to this brain (Rorden 2012), so the inner surface follows the brain; the foramen magnum lets the medulla through and the optic canals the optic nerves. Calvarial thickness on CT averaged about 8 mm in the frontal, 7 mm in the parietal, 4.7 mm in the temporal and 8 mm in the occipital bone in 100 adults (Thulung 2019). The jaws below the template's field of view are drawn with typical proportions.
skull.lesion: A fracture of the thin temporal bone at the pterion can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an epidural haematoma (often a lucid interval, then rapid decline). Fractures of the skull base cause bruising around the eyes (raccoon eyes) or behind the ear (Battle sign) and leakage of CSF from the nose or ear.

mandible.note: The only movable bone of the skull: a horseshoe-shaped body carrying the lower teeth and two rami rising to the condyles, which form the temporomandibular joints in front of the ear, and to the coronoid processes, where the temporalis muscle inserts. The mental foramen below the premolars lets out the mental nerve, the end of the inferior alveolar branch of the mandibular nerve (V3). Drawn shape with typical proportions.
mandible.lesion: Fractures often break the ring in two places, for example the body on one side and the condyle on the other. Numbness of the chin and lower lip (numb chin syndrome) can signal a lesion of the inferior alveolar or mental nerve, including a metastasis.

teeth.note: Thirty-two permanent teeth: in each quarter of the mouth two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. The upper teeth are supplied by the maxillary nerve (V2) and the lower teeth by the inferior alveolar branch of the mandibular nerve (V3). Crowns drawn with typical sizes.
teeth.lesion: Because tooth pain travels in the trigeminal nerve, dental pain and trigeminal pain can be confused.

systems.d: Emotion, motivation and memory: a ring of structures around the brain's core (Papez circuit and its extensions), joined by the fornix and the cingulum bundle. The mammillary bodies belong here but are not separately labelled in this atlas.
Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra project to the caudate and putamen. Their loss causes Parkinson's disease; D2 blockade by antipsychotics here causes stiffness and tremor.
Cortex to striatum to globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, back through the thalamus to the cortex: selects and scales movements. The deep brain stimulation targets lie here.

systems.n: Midbrain dopamine pathways to striatum and cortex
systems.d: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra project to the striatum and to prefrontal and limbic cortex. In schizophrenia, PET studies find raised presynaptic dopamine mainly in the associative (dorsal) striatum rather than the limbic (ventral) striatum, which argues against the older 'mesolimbic' version of the dopamine hypothesis.

Active when we rest, remember our past, imagine the future or think about ourselves. Its core is the cortical midline (medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate/precuneus); the extended network adds the angular gyrus and medial temporal lobe.

Detects what matters right now, from the body and the world, and switches the brain between inward and outward attention. Defined from brain imaging; core nodes are the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate.

A proposed functional model, not an anatomical tract: the motor system sends a copy of each command (corollary discharge) so the brain can predict and recognise the result as self-made. Failures are a leading explanation of passivity experiences in schizophrenia.

Plans, starts and coordinates movement: from the motor cortex down the corticospinal tract through the internal capsule and brainstem to the motor neurons of the brainstem and spinal cord (both affected in ALS).

In most people language depends mainly on the left hemisphere: comprehension at the back (posterior superior temporal cortex) and production at the front (Broca's area), joined by the arcuate fasciculus (part of the superior longitudinal fasciculus). Shown on the left side only.
Forms and retrieves memories of events: the hippocampus and its inputs, the fornix, the thalamus and cingulate (Papez circuit). The first system affected in typical Alzheimer's disease.
Keeps goals in mind and controls attention: lateral prefrontal and parietal cortex. Defined from brain imaging.

From the optic nerves and chiasm along the optic tracts (schematic) to the lateral geniculate nucleus, through the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex, then outward to areas for shape, faces, words and motion. A side branch to the superior colliculus turns the eyes towards things.

From the cochlear nuclei through the brainstem to the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate nucleus, then through the acoustic radiation to Heschl's gyrus and the speech and voice areas of the superior temporal cortex.
Nuclei that move the eyes (III, IV, VI) and the structures that coordinate them: vestibular nuclei, superior colliculus, frontal eye field (in the middle frontal gyrus) and cerebellar vermis.

The brainstem nuclei of cranial nerves III to XII (schematic positions). Cranial nerves I (smell) and II (vision) are not brainstem nerves: they grow out of the forebrain. The spinal accessory nucleus (XI) lies in the upper spinal cord, which is not drawn.
Serotonin neurons of the raphe nuclei in the brainstem project to almost the whole forebrain; SSRIs and other antidepressants act on this system.

The twelve pairs of cranial nerves with the optic tract, drawn along schematic intracranial courses from where they leave the brain to the skull base. Use the nerve buttons in the 3D view to show them alone with the brainstem.

systems.n: Cranial nerves with their brainstem nuclei
systems.d: Each nerve in the same colour as its nucleus (schematic), so you can follow a nerve back into the brainstem.

The ring of arteries under the brain that links the two carotid systems with the vertebrobasilar system: internal carotid arteries, A1 segments, anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating arteries and P1 segments. This model shows one complete, symmetric configuration; variants are not drawn yet. A complete circle is found in only about a third to a half of people. The basilar artery feeds the circle from behind but is not part of the ring.
The anterior (carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulations with their main branches and segments. Teaching model of the typical configuration.

nt.d: The signal of movement, motivation and reward learning: from the midbrain along four classic pathways.

routes.d: Movement selection; these neurons are lost in Parkinson's disease.
Reward, motivation and learning from outcomes.

nt.rec: D1-like (D1, D5) and D2-like (D2, D3, D4) receptors, all G-protein coupled. A fourth pathway, tuberoinfundibular (hypothalamus to pituitary, inhibits prolactin), is not drawn because the pituitary is not in the model.
nt.drugs: Levodopa and dopamine agonists (Parkinson's disease); antipsychotics block D2 receptors; stimulants raise synaptic dopamine.

nt.d: A modulator from the raphe nuclei along the brainstem midline to almost the whole brain: mood, sleep, pain, impulse control.

routes.d: The rostral raphe group projects mainly to the forebrain.
Parallel, overlapping forebrain projections. The caudal raphe group (not drawn) projects to the brainstem and spinal cord.

nt.rec: Seven receptor families (5-HT1 to 5-HT7); 5-HT3 is an ion channel, the others are G-protein coupled.
nt.drugs: SSRIs and SNRIs (depression, anxiety); triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists, migraine); ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist, nausea); many atypical antipsychotics block 5-HT2A.

nt.d: Arousal and attention from a tiny nucleus in the rostral pons, the locus coeruleus, to the cortex, thalamus, hippocampus and cerebellum.

routes.d: Widespread forebrain innervation: alertness, attention, stress response.
Cerebellar and spinal projections (spinal cord not in the model).

nt.rec: Alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta (beta-1 to beta-3) adrenergic receptors, all G-protein coupled. The locus coeruleus position is schematic (probabilistic MRI map: Keren et al. 2009).
nt.drugs: SNRIs and atomoxetine block reuptake; clonidine and guanfacine are alpha-2 agonists; beta-blockers act on beta receptors.

nt.d: Attention, learning and memory: from the basal forebrain to the cortex and hippocampus, and from the brainstem to the thalamus.

routes.d: Nucleus basalis: cortical attention and plasticity; degenerates early in Alzheimer's disease.
Septohippocampal projection (septum shown within the basal forebrain label): memory.
Pedunculopontine nucleus: arousal and REM sleep, gait.

nt.rec: Nicotinic receptors (ion channels) and muscarinic receptors M1 to M5 (G-protein coupled). Striatal cholinergic interneurons are local and not drawn.
nt.drugs: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) in Alzheimer's disease; anticholinergic drugs can cause confusion in older people.

nt.d: The main excitatory transmitter: the projection neurons of the cortex, thalamus and hippocampus use it.

routes.d: Voluntary movement; the drawn line ends in the medulla (spinal cord not in the model).
Cortex drives the striatum, the input of the basal ganglia.
The thalamus relays sensation and motor loops to the cortex.

nt.rec: Ion channels (AMPA, NMDA, kainate) and metabotropic receptors (mGluR1 to mGluR8).
nt.drugs: Memantine (NMDA antagonist, Alzheimer's disease); ketamine and esketamine (NMDA antagonists, treatment-resistant depression); riluzole (ALS); perampanel (AMPA antagonist, epilepsy).

nt.d: The main inhibitory transmitter: mostly local interneurons; its long pathways are the outputs of the striatum, pallidum and cerebellar cortex.

routes.n: Striatum to pallidum and substantia nigra
routes.d: Direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways.
The inhibitory output of the basal ganglia.
Purkinje cells inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei (inside the cerebellar white matter; nuclei not modelled separately).

nt.rec: GABA-A receptors (chloride channels; benzodiazepine site) and GABA-B receptors (G-protein coupled).
nt.drugs: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates enhance GABA-A; baclofen is a GABA-B agonist; several antiseizure drugs act on GABA.

nt.d: A wakefulness signal: all brain histamine neurons sit in the tuberomammillary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus.

routes.d: Active only during waking; maintains wakefulness and attention.

nt.rec: H1 and H2 (mostly excitatory), H3 (inhibitory autoreceptor and heteroreceptor); H4 mainly outside the brain. Position schematic.
nt.drugs: Sedating antihistamines block H1; pitolisant (H3 inverse agonist) treats narcolepsy; H1 blockade contributes to sedation and weight gain with some psychotropic drugs.

nt.d: A wakefulness stabiliser from the lateral hypothalamus that drives the other arousal nuclei; its loss causes narcolepsy type 1.

routes.d: Keeps the monoamine and cholinergic arousal systems switched on together.

nt.rec: OX1 and OX2 receptors (G-protein coupled). Position schematic.
nt.drugs: Orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant, daridorexant) treat insomnia.

pathgroups.d: Link the cortex with the deep brain, brainstem and spinal cord.
From the eye to the visual cortex.
The twelve pairs with schematic intracranial courses.

The arterial ring under the brain: internal carotid arteries, A1 segments, anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating arteries and P1 segments (typical complete form). The basilar artery feeds it from behind.
Internal carotid artery and its branches: anterior and middle cerebral arteries, segment by segment.
Vertebral and basilar arteries, the cerebellar arteries and the posterior cerebral artery.

pathgroups.n: Long pathways: brain to spinal cord
pathgroups.d: Six long pathways drawn through the brainstem, cerebellum and spinal cord. Blue fibres start on the left and orange fibres on the right, so the colours swap sides where a pathway crosses the midline; white markers show each crossing.

networks.d: Occipital visual areas: from the first analysis of the image to objects and motion.
Moving and feeling the body along the central sulcus; in the Yeo map it also includes auditory cortex.
Goal-directed attention: intraparietal sulcus, frontal eye fields and motion area MT+; selects where to look.
Anterior insula, anterior cingulate and temporoparietal junction: notices what matters and helps switch between networks.

Orbitofrontal cortex and temporal pole only. Despite the name it is not the classic limbic system: hippocampus, amygdala and cingulate are not part of it. These areas lie near the air-filled sinuses, where the MRI signal is weak and distorted, so this is the least certain network, partly for technical reasons.
Lateral prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex: flexible control, working memory and problem solving.
Medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate and precuneus, angular gyrus and lateral temporal cortex: memory, imagining and thinking about oneself and others.

network_note: Networks from resting-state functional MRI of 1,000 people (Yeo et al. 2011), here from the Schaefer 2018 400-parcel version in the same template space, painted on the 3D cortex (nearest parcel within 4 mm). Networks are statistical groupings of areas that are active together, not anatomical structures; borders differ between people.
